Coherent multi-population models

Source: R/model-multipop.R
li_lee.Rd

Joint models for several strata (for example women and men, or regions) whose forecasts do not diverge in the long run:

Usage

li_lee(ratio_order = 1, common_by = NULL, jump_off = c("fitted", "observed"))

product_ratio(ratio_order = 1, jump_off = c("fitted", "observed"))

Arguments

ratio_order

Number of stratum-specific (ratio) factors.

common_by

Stratum variable(s) defining groups with their own common factor (li_lee() only).

jump_off

"fitted" (forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year) or "observed" (forecasts are multiplied by the ratio of observed to fitted rates in the last year, per age and stratum; Lee and Miller 2001). With few factors per stratum the fitted rates of the last year can be far from the observed ones; the observed jump-off then avoids a step between the last observed and the first forecast year.

Value

A model specification.

Details

  • li_lee() (Li and Lee 2005): log m[x,t,i] = a[x,i] + B[x] K[t] + b[x,i] k[t,i]. The common factor B K is a Lee-Carter model of the pooled rates (sum of deaths over sum of exposures); the stratum factors b k are fitted to the residuals.

  • product_ratio() (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013): the geometric mean of the stratum rates (product) is modelled with a Lee-Carter-type factor, and the ratios of each stratum to the product with factors whose scores are stationary. This is a Lee-Carter-type version of the method; the original uses functional data models.

With common_by (for example "sex"), li_lee() fits one common factor per level of that stratum variable (women and men each with their own trend), and the other strata (for example regions and deprivation quintiles) deviate from their group's common factor. If the data carry a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()), the common factors are estimated from the bottom strata only, so aggregates are not counted twice.

In both models the common period index follows a random walk with drift (with drift uncertainty) and the stratum-specific scores follow AR(1) processes without drift, so the differences between strata stay bounded. Draws include the innovations of all indexes; predictive draws add extra-Poisson and Poisson variation.

References

Li N, Lee R (2005). Coherent mortality forecasts for a group of populations: an extension of the Lee-Carter method. Demography 42(3): 575-594. doi:10.1353/dem.2005.0021

Lee R, Miller T (2001). Evaluating the performance of the Lee-Carter method for forecasting mortality. Demography 38(4): 537-549.

Hyndman RJ, Booth H, Yasmeen F (2013). Coherent mortality forecasting: the product-ratio method with functional time series models. Demography 50(1): 261-283.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
